implementation_notes: Java's abstract class is the direct realization: shared fields and implemented methods live on the superclass, members each layer type must supply are declared abstract, and the compiler forbids instantiating the base or leaving an abstract member unimplemented. Keep the constructor protected, mark invariant methods final so subclasses cannot break them, and name the type from the layer's vocabulary (DomainObject, AbstractMapper, ApplicationController). When the layer shares behavior but no state an interface with default methods supplies the implementation without spending the single superclass slot; for ORM-mapped layers @MappedSuperclass makes the base contribute persistent fields (id, version, timestamps) into every subclass's own table without becoming an entity.
pitfalls: Virtual calls made from the superclass constructor run before the subclass's fields are initialised - the classic Java base-class trap.
protected fields and non-final methods widen the contract every subclass depends on; adding a method to the base can silently change the behavior of subclasses that already define a matching method.
Java permits only one superclass: when a framework base is also required, the layer contract has to move to an interface.

variants.name: Layer interface with default methods
variants.implementation_notes: When the layer's contract carries no state, declare the layer type as an interface whose default methods hold the shared implementation and let each member implement the interface, keeping the single class slot free for a framework base or a domain superclass. Default methods are inherited by implementing classes and may be overridden, and conflicts between unrelated interfaces must be resolved by an explicit override that calls Interface.super.method(). The limitation is structural: interfaces cannot hold instance state, so identity counters, caches and other shared fields cannot live here.
pitfalls: Diamond conflicts between two interfaces' default methods are a compile error until the class overrides and invokes Interface.super.method() explicitly.
Interfaces cannot hold instance state, so a layer that shares version counters, caches or other fields cannot be built on defaults alone.
Only the interface path reaches a default member: code holding a class reference that does not redeclare it will not see it.

variants.name: @MappedSuperclass entity base (JPA)
variants.implementation_notes: For persistence layers the supertype is annotated @MappedSuperclass: its persistent fields and mapping annotations are inherited by every entity that extends it and are mapped into each entity's own table, while the base itself is not an entity and has no table. It is the framework-sanctioned home for the id, version and audit columns shared by all entities, and subclasses may override inherited mappings with @AttributeOverride or @AssociationOverride. Because it cannot be queried, passed to EntityManager methods or be the target of a relationship, treat it as a mapping carrier rather than a domain participant.
pitfalls: @MappedSuperclass is not an entity: it cannot be queried, used in EntityManager operations or be the target of an association, which surprises code that treats the base as the layer's runtime type.
Inherited mappings are applied in the context of each subclass table, so a column/attribute name collision between the base and a subclass fails at schema generation or startup.
Mapping annotations in a plain (non-mapped) superclass are ignored entirely, so an unannotated base silently loses its persistent fields.
